config.title: Debounced Search

intro.title: Debounced Search
intro.body: In this lesson, you will build a search input component that fetches and displays results from an API only after the user has stopped typing for a short moment. You will learn the concept of debouncing, which helps improve performance by delaying a function call until after a pause in user input. The main technologies involved are React's useState and useEffect hooks, along with a custom debounce function implemented in TypeScript. This project will teach you how to manage user input efficiently and make controlled API calls.
intro.usecase: Debounced search is essential in any UI where users type to filter or search through data, preventing excessive API calls and improving performance. You'll see this pattern in e-commerce product filters, admin dashboards with real-time data tables, and search bars for large datasets like user directories or content libraries. As a developer, implementing debounced search ensures your applications remain responsive while handling user input efficiently, especially when dealing with backend APIs or computationally expensive filtering operations.

objectives: Apply TypeScript interfaces to define the structure of search result data
Implement React state hooks to manage the search query and results
Utilize the useEffect hook to trigger side effects when the query changes
Construct a debounce function to delay API calls and prevent excessive requests
Use setTimeout and clearTimeout to control the timing of function execution
Handle input change events to update the search query state
Define a fetch function to retrieve search results from an API endpoint
Apply conditional rendering to display loading states and search results
Modify component cleanup to clear pending timeouts and prevent memory leaks
Return structured JSX with input fields and result lists for the search interface

steps.title: Import React and useState from 'react'
steps.instruction: Import React and the useState hook from the 'react' package.
steps.hint: Use the import statement to bring in React and useState from 'react'.
steps.analogousExample:
// Example of importing React and useState from 'react'
import React, { useState } from 'react';
steps.expectedOutcome: The 'react' package is imported with React and useState available for use.
successCriteria: The code includes an import statement that imports React and useState from 'react'.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully imported React and useState from 'react'. This gives you access to React's core functionality and the useState hook for managing state.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but the import statement needs adjustment. Make sure you're importing both React and useState from 'react'.
steps.feedbackWrong: The import statement is missing or incorrect. You need to import React and useState from 'react' to proceed.

steps.title: Import useRef and useEffect from 'react'
steps.instruction: Import the useRef and useEffect hooks from the 'react' package.
steps.hint: Add an import statement that brings in both useRef and useEffect from 'react'.
steps.analogousExample:
// Example of importing hooks from React
import { useRef, useEffect } from 'react';
steps.expectedOutcome: The code will have both useRef and useEffect available for use in the component.
successCriteria: The import statement includes both useRef and useEffect from the 'react' package.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully imported both useRef and useEffect hooks. These will be essential for managing timers and side effects in your debounced search.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close, but you need to import both useRef and useEffect from 'react'. Check that you have both hooks in your import statement.
steps.feedbackWrong: This step requires importing both useRef and useEffect hooks from the 'react' package. Make sure your import statement includes both.

steps.title: Create the main SearchComponent
steps.instruction: Create a functional component named SearchComponent that returns JSX.Element. Use either a function declaration or arrow function syntax.
steps.hint: Define a component that returns a JSX element. For TypeScript, specify the return type as JSX.Element.
steps.expectedOutcome: A functional component named SearchComponent is defined with JSX.Element return type.
successCriteria: The code should define a component named SearchComponent that returns JSX.Element. It can be either a function declaration or arrow function.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully created the SearchComponent functional component with proper TypeScript typing.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure your component is named exactly 'SearchComponent' and returns JSX.Element.
steps.feedbackWrong: The component definition is missing or incorrect. Remember to create a functional component named SearchComponent that returns JSX.Element.

steps.title: Initialize search query state
steps.instruction: Inside your SearchComponent, initialize a state variable named 'query' using useState, with an empty string as the default value.
steps.hint: Use the useState hook you imported earlier. Remember to specify the type as string.
steps.analogousExample:
// Example of initializing a string state variable
const [query, setQuery] = useState<string>('');
steps.expectedOutcome: Your component will have a state variable 'query' that can store the current search input value.
successCriteria: The code should include a useState call that declares a 'query' state variable with an empty string default value.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully initialized the search query state. This will allow your component to track what the user types in the search field.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure you're using useState with the correct syntax and type. The state variable should be named 'query' and initialized with an empty string.
steps.feedbackWrong: Let's try again. You need to use the useState hook to create a state variable named 'query' that starts as an empty string. Remember to use TypeScript syntax to specify the string type.

steps.title: Initialize search results state
steps.instruction: Inside your SearchComponent, initialize a state variable named 'results' using useState. Set its default value to an empty array of strings.
steps.hint: Use the useState hook with a type annotation for string[] to create the results state.
steps.analogousExample:
// Example of initializing a state variable for an array of strings
const [items, setItems] = useState<string[]>([]);
steps.expectedOutcome: The component will have a state variable 'results' initialized as an empty array of strings, ready to store search results.
successCriteria: The code must include a useState call for 'results' with the correct type annotation (string[]) and default value (empty array).
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully initialized the results state. This array will hold the search results we fetch later.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but check that your state variable is named 'results' and has the correct type annotation (string[]) with an empty array as the default value.
steps.feedbackWrong: The results state isn't properly initialized. Make sure you're using useState with the correct type and default value for an array of strings.

steps.title: Create a ref for the timer
steps.instruction: Inside your SearchComponent, create a ref named 'timeoutRef' using the useRef hook. Initialize it with null.
steps.hint: Use the useRef hook you imported earlier. The ref will store the timeout ID for the debounced search.
steps.analogousExample:
// Example of creating a ref with useRef
const timerRef = useRef<number | null>(null);
steps.expectedOutcome: The component will have a ref variable named 'timeoutRef' that can store a timeout ID.
successCriteria: The code should include a useRef call that creates a ref named 'timeoutRef' initialized to null.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully created a ref to store the timeout ID. This ref will help us manage the debounce timer.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure you're using the useRef hook to create a ref named 'timeoutRef' and initializing it with null.
steps.feedbackWrong: Let's try again. You need to create a ref using the useRef hook. Name it 'timeoutRef' and initialize it with null.

steps.title: Define the handleSearchChange handler
steps.instruction: Inside your SearchComponent, define a function named handleSearchChange that takes a React.ChangeEvent<HTMLInputElement> parameter and updates the query state with the input's current value.
steps.hint: Create a function that receives an event parameter and calls setQuery with event.target.value.
steps.expectedOutcome: A handleSearchChange function is defined that updates the query state when called with an input change event.
successCriteria: The function should be named handleSearchChange, accept a React.ChangeEvent<HTMLInputElement> parameter, and call setQuery with event.target.value.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully defined the typed change handler that will update the query state.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close! Make sure your function is named handleSearchChange, accepts a React.ChangeEvent<HTMLInputElement> parameter, and calls setQuery with the input value.
steps.feedbackWrong: The function definition doesn't match the requirements. It should be named handleSearchChange, accept a React.ChangeEvent<HTMLInputElement> parameter, and update the query state with the input value.

steps.title: Define the performSearch function
steps.instruction: Define a function named performSearch inside your component. This function should simulate an API call by updating the results state with mock data based on the current query value.
steps.hint: Create a regular function or arrow function called performSearch. Inside it, you can update the results state with an array containing mock search results.
steps.expectedOutcome: You should have a performSearch function defined inside your component that updates the results state with mock data.
successCriteria: Function updates results state with mock data
Function uses setResults to update state
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully defined the performSearch function that simulates an API call by updating the results state with mock data.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure your performSearch function properly updates the results state with mock data. Check that you're using setResults to update the state.
steps.feedbackWrong: The performSearch function isn't defined correctly. Make sure you create a function named performSearch that updates the results state with mock search results.

steps.title: Set up the debouncing effect
steps.instruction: Create a useEffect hook that sets a timeout to call performSearch after 500ms when the query changes, and clears the previous timeout on cleanup.
steps.hint: The useEffect should depend on the query state and use the timerRef to manage the timeout.
steps.expectedOutcome: The useEffect hook is added with proper dependency array and cleanup function that clears the timeout.
successCriteria:
The code includes a useEffect hook that:
1. Has a dependency array containing [query]
2. Clears any existing timeout using timerRef.current
3. Sets a new timeout that calls performSearch after 500ms
4. Returns a cleanup function that clears the timeout
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully implemented the debouncing effect. The useEffect will now trigger performSearch only after the user stops typing for 500ms.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but check if your useEffect includes all required parts: dependency on query, clearing existing timeout, setting new timeout with performSearch, and cleanup function.
steps.feedbackWrong: The useEffect implementation is missing key elements. Review the example and ensure you have the dependency array, timeout management, and cleanup function.

steps.title: Return the main container structure
steps.instruction: Inside your SearchComponent's return statement, replace the existing div with a new div container that contains an h1 heading with text 'Debounced Search' and an input element.
steps.hint: The JSX structure should be: a div containing an h1 and an input element. The input element can be self-closing (<input />).
steps.expectedOutcome: The component now returns a basic JSX structure with a heading and an input element, ready for wiring up functionality in later steps.
successCriteria: The return statement contains a div container
The div contains an h1 element with text 'Debounced Search'
The div contains an input element
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully created the basic container structure with a heading and input field. This provides the foundation for the search UI.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure your return statement includes: 1) a div container, 2) an h1 with the text 'Debounced Search', and 3) an input element. All three elements should be present.
steps.feedbackWrong: The return statement doesn't match the required structure. You need to return a div containing an h1 with text 'Debounced Search' and an input element.

steps.title: Wire the input to query state and handler
steps.instruction: Add the value and onChange props to the input element to connect it to your query state and change handler.
steps.hint: Set value={query} and onChange={handleSearchChange} on the input element.
steps.expectedOutcome: The input element will be connected to the query state and update it when the user types.
successCriteria: The input element should have both value={query} and onChange={handleSearchChange} attributes.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully connected the input to your state and handler. The input now displays the current query value and updates it when the user types.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but you need both value and onChange attributes. Make sure you have value={query} and onChange={handleSearchChange} on the input element.
steps.feedbackWrong: The input element isn't properly connected. You need to add both value={query} and onChange={handleSearchChange} attributes to the input.

steps.title: Display the search results
steps.instruction: In the component's return statement, add a section below the input to display the search results. Map over the 'results' state array to render each result as a list item inside an unordered list.
steps.hint: Use the 'results' state variable and map() to create list items. Place this after the input element.
steps.expectedOutcome: The component will now display the search results in an unordered list below the input field.
successCriteria: The return statement includes an unordered list (<ul>) that maps over the 'results' state array to render list items (<li>) for each result.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully added the results display section. The search results will now be visible in the UI when the results array contains items.
steps.feedbackPartial: You've added some structure for displaying results, but it doesn't fully match what's needed. Make sure you're using the 'results' state variable and mapping over it to create list items inside an unordered list.
steps.feedbackWrong: The results display section is missing or incorrect. You need to add an unordered list that maps over the 'results' state array to display each result as a list item.
